reference.source: Volpe's Neurology of the Newborn / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: The most severe congenital muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy, defined by the triad of a brain malformation (cobblestone lissencephaly), eye anomalies, and congenital muscular dystrophy
Cobblestone (type II) lissencephaly results from over-migration of neurons beyond the pial surface, producing a bumpy, disorganised cortex distinct from classic lissencephaly
Neuroimaging typically shows cobblestone cortex, hydrocephalus, a kinked or hypoplastic brainstem (the Z-shaped brainstem), and cerebellar hypoplasia or cysts
Ocular malformations are prominent and may include microphthalmia, cataract, retinal dysplasia or detachment, persistent foetal vasculature, and anterior chamber anomalies
The congenital muscular dystrophy causes marked hypotonia and weakness from birth with a raised serum creatine kinase
It is autosomal recessive, caused by variants in genes for O-glycosylation of alpha-dystroglycan such as POMT1, POMT2, and FKTN, disrupting the dystroglycan-extracellular matrix link
Diagnosis integrates the characteristic MRI, ophthalmological findings, raised creatine kinase, and molecular testing of dystroglycanopathy genes
reference.pathophysiology: Walker-Warburg syndrome is a dystroglycanopathy caused by biallelic variants in genes required for O-linked glycosylation of alpha-dystroglycan. Defective glycosylation prevents alpha-dystroglycan from binding extracellular matrix ligands such as laminin, disrupting the integrity of basement membranes. In the developing brain, breaches of the pial-glial limiting membrane allow neurons to over-migrate beyond the cortex, producing cobblestone lissencephaly, brainstem and cerebellar malformation, and hydrocephalus. The same defect impairs the muscle basement membrane, causing congenital muscular dystrophy, and disrupts ocular development, causing the retinal and anterior segment anomalies.
additionalDifferentials: Muscle-eye-brain disease, a milder dystroglycanopathy on the same spectrum
Classic (type I) lissencephaly from LIS1 or DCX
Other congenital muscular dystrophies with brain involvement
Congenital infection causing brain and eye malformation
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI for cobblestone cortex, brainstem kinking, cerebellar anomaly, and hydrocephalus
Serum creatine kinase, which is characteristically elevated
Detailed ophthalmological examination for retinal dysplasia and anterior segment anomalies
Molecular genetic testing of dystroglycanopathy genes such as POMT1, POMT2, and FKTN
Muscle biopsy with alpha-dystroglycan glycosylation studies where genetics are inconclusive
Prenatal ultrasound and foetal MRI for hydrocephalus and brain malformation in at-risk pregnancies
redFlags: Severe respiratory and feeding difficulty from profound muscle weakness
Rapidly progressive visual loss from retinal detachment
reference.prognosis: Walker-Warburg syndrome carries the worst prognosis of the dystroglycanopathies, with most affected children dying within the first years of life from neurological, respiratory, and feeding complications. Care is largely supportive alongside genetic counselling.
pitfalls: Confusing cobblestone (type II) lissencephaly with classic (type I) lissencephaly, which has different genetics and no primary muscle or eye disease
Overlooking the raised creatine kinase and muscle involvement when focused on the brain malformation
Missing treatable ocular complications such as retinal detachment
Failing to place the child on the dystroglycanopathy spectrum, affecting prognosis and counselling
management: Recognise there is no disease-modifying therapy and centre care on supportive and palliative management given the very poor prognosis
Treat hydrocephalus with ventriculoperitoneal shunting to relieve raised intracranial pressure
Support nutrition and airway protection with gastrostomy feeding for swallowing difficulty and recurrent aspiration
Provide respiratory support and prompt treatment of intercurrent chest infections
Refer to ophthalmology for treatable ocular anomalies such as cataract and retinal detachment
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance with prenatal diagnosis in at-risk pregnancies, and involve paediatric neurodisability and palliative care teams
